title: The Trap I Walked Into
scene: During a friendly shogi game, a player sees what looks like a free piece and takes it. Two moves later, he realizes he has fallen into a trap. He praises his friend, who admits the trap was a gamble.
sceneJa: 友人との将棋で、簡単に取れそうな駒を見つけた。相手のミスだと思って取るが、二手後に罠だったと気づく。相手の巧みさを認めると、本人も成功するかは分からなかったと笑う。

chunks.ja: 友人との気軽な将棋で

chunks.en: a clear way to attack his king.
chunks.ja: 相手の王を攻める明快な手を

chunks.en: where I could easily take it.
chunks.ja: 僕が簡単に取れる場所に
それで、まんまと誘いに乗ってしまった

chunks.en: I'd walked right into his trap.
chunks.ja: 相手の罠にまんまとはまったことに

chunks.en: 'I have to hand it to you—
chunks.ja: 「これは君を認めざるを得ないよ

chunks.en: I wasn't sure you'd take it.'
chunks.ja: 君が取ってくれるか、自信はなかったんだ」

questions.question: Which split keeps the idiom together and follows natural speaking units?
options: Two moves later / I realized / I'd walked right into his trap.
Two moves / later I realized I'd / walked right into / his trap.
Two / moves later I realized / I'd walked right / into his trap.
questions.explanation: 'Walked right into his trap' is a complete idiomatic unit. Pause after the time phrase, then after 'I realized'.

questions.question: What does 'I took the bait' mean in this shogi story?
options: I picked up food from the table.
I deliberately ignored a tempting move.
I accepted a tempting move and fell for a trap.
questions.explanation: 'Take the bait' means respond to a tempting offer or provocation. Here, the apparent free piece was a lure.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say 'I have to hand it to you'?
options: He is asking for his piece back.
He is acknowledging his friend's skill, despite losing.
He is saying the game must end immediately.
questions.explanation: 'Have to hand it to someone' expresses respect or admiration for what they did, even when you were the one who lost.

speak: Imagine a friendly game or small competition where you fell for a trick. Imagine: see the apparently free piece. Read: follow the change from confidence to respect. Chunk: say 'I took the bait', 'I walked right into a trap', and 'I have to hand it to you' as whole units. Understand: the first two admit a mistake; the last praises someone else. Check: answer three questions. Speak (30 seconds): describe the tempting move, explain the trap, and praise your opponent using those three chunks. Final Read: read the six sentences without Japanese; sound confident at first, surprised at the trap, then genuinely impressed. Pause lightly before 'For what it's worth'.
review: New: 'take the bait' (誘いに乗る・罠に引っかかる), 'walk right into a trap' (まんまと罠にはまる), 'I have to hand it to you' (君には感心する・腕前を認める). Reuse Lesson 94 'I could've sworn ...' (絶対に〜だと思った) for a mistaken shogi judgment rather than missing coffee; Lesson 93/102 'For what it's worth' (一応言っておくと) for a wry admission rather than a gentle opinion about a concert or soup. Also 'for a moment' from Lesson 95. The latest 14 lessons 91–104 covered routines, invitations, museums, food, and planning; this one teaches graciously acknowledging an opponent after a tactical mistake, not another scheduling or food misunderstanding.
